**ARGUMENT**

**I. Article 35's two-year period is a condition precedent, but it is not immune from equitable considerations, and in any event the airline's bankruptcy stay tolled it.**

**A. Article 35 sets a condition precedent whose operation the forum's law may inform.**

Article 35(1) of the Montreal Convention provides that the "right to damages shall be extinguished if an action is not brought within a period of two years." Article 35(2) adds that "[t]he method of calculating that period shall be determined by the law of the court seized of the case." Plaintiff does not dispute that Article 35 is a condition precedent to suit rather than an ordinary statute of limitations. But characterizing a deadline as a condition precedent does not answer whether the forum may account for circumstances that suspend or interrupt the running of the period. Article 35(2) expressly delegates the "method of calculating" the period to the forum, and the Eleventh Circuit's tolling doctrine is part of that law.

The Eleventh Circuit applies equitable tolling where a litigant's untimeliness results from "extraordinary circumstances that are both beyond his control and unavoidable even with diligence." *Sandvik v. United States*, 177 F.3d 1269, [1271] (11th Cir. 1999); *see also Justice v. United States*, 6 F.3d 1474, [1479] (11th Cir. 1993). The doctrine rests on the premise that a filing deadline should not be applied mechanically where the plaintiff diligently pursued the claim and was prevented from filing. *See Arce v. Garcia*, 434 F.3d 1254, [1261] (11th Cir. 2006); *Steed v. Head*, 219 F.3d 1298, [1300] (11th Cir. 2000); *Cadet v. Bulger*, 377 F.3d 1173, [1184–85] (11th Cir. 2004). Nothing in the Convention's text displaces that background rule. Article 35(2) points toward it. The Eleventh Circuit has also treated Montreal Convention questions under ordinary principles of treaty interpretation, giving effect to the text and to the forum-law references the drafters chose to include. *See Campbell v. Air Jamaica Ltd.*, 863 F.3d 1255, [pin cite] (11th Cir. 2017).

**B. Plaintiff's circumstances warrant equitable consideration.**

[Insert record facts: date of the incident; date the airline filed for bankruptcy; when Plaintiff learned of the filing; steps Plaintiff took to preserve the claim, such as a proof of claim, stay-relief inquiry, or contact with the claims administrator; and the date suit was filed.] Plaintiff acted diligently. The obstacle was the airline's bankruptcy filing, an event wholly outside Plaintiff's control. Under *Sandvik* and *Justice*, those are the circumstances that justify tolling. The airline suffers no cognizable prejudice, because it was on notice of the claim and the bankruptcy process itself preserved the evidence and the claim.

**C. Alternatively, the automatic stay tolled the period.**

The filing of a bankruptcy petition operates as a stay of "the commencement or continuation" of any action against the debtor that was or could have been commenced before the petition. 11 U.S.C. § 362(a)(1). Section 108(c) of the Bankruptcy Code extends a nonbankruptcy limitations period that has not expired before the petition until the later of the period's end or thirty days after notice of termination or expiration of the stay. 11 U.S.C. § 108(c). Because Article 35(2) commits the method of calculation to the law of the forum, and that law includes federal bankruptcy law, the stay and § 108(c) operate on the Article 35 period. Any other result would extinguish a claim because Plaintiff obeyed a federal statutory injunction. [Add Eleventh Circuit and Supremacy Clause authority on the interaction of § 108(c) with treaty-based periods, after confirming that such authority exists.] The airline cannot invoke the stay to bar Plaintiff's suit and then invoke the passage of time that the stay itself caused.

**D. Conclusion.**

The district court treated Article 35 as an absolute bar. It should have applied the forum's tolling principles under Article 35(2) and the stay and extension provisions of §§ 362(a) and 108(c). The judgment should be reversed and the case remanded for a determination of timeliness under those standards.
